narrative:
The system estimates there is a 67% chance you will leave your job in the near future, which is why the promotion was denied. This prediction is based on patterns observed in similar employees, focusing on factors that most strongly indicate whether someone is likely to stay or go.

The most significant factor pushing you toward leaving is that you’ve received other job opportunities while working here. Employees who explore external options are far more likely to resign, and this was the strongest signal in your case. On the other hand, two factors worked in your favor: you feel you’ve received the promotions you deserved, and you’ve spent 6–10 years in your current role—both of which typically suggest higher loyalty. However, these positive influences weren’t enough to outweigh the risk indicated by the job opportunities you’ve encountered.

Other aspects of your profile also played a role. For example, while you’re satisfied with your job overall and feel recognized for your work, you haven’t attended any training programs in the last three years, and you don’t find the ones offered particularly useful. Additionally, you don’t feel a strong sense of job stability, which can make employees more open to leaving. Your salary, experience level, and sector are in line with many who were promoted, but these other factors raised concerns.

To improve your chances in the future, focus on deepening your commitment to the organization. Engaging in training programs—especially those you find valuable—could signal your long-term interest. Addressing any lingering concerns about job security, whether through conversations with management or by seeking clarity on your career path, may also help. The system will reassess your profile over time, so demonstrating stability and growth in these areas could strengthen your case for future opportunities.
